list.listitem: Perform a 12-lead ECG and obtain cardiac biomarkers promptly in all patients with chest discomfort consistent with possible acute coronary syndrome (ACS). B
Give 165 to 325 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin to all patients with possible unstable angina. B
Patients with symptoms of possible ACS should be transported via EMS to a hospital for evaluation. B
Give oxygen and sublingual nitroglycerin for early treatment of suspected unstable angina; morphine may be a useful adjunct. B
An early invasive strategy is indicated in unstable angina/non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction (UA/NSTEMI) patients who have refractory angina or hemodynamic or electrical instability. B

background.definition: The American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) define unstable angina as part of the spectrum of ACS. A clinical diagnosis is made on the basis of angina that is new or increasing or occurring at rest. With the increasing use of high sensitivity troponin, patients with unstable angina are increasingly reclassified as non-ST elevation MI (NSTEMI).

list.listitem: Nearly 1 million patients each year have a primary diagnosis of unstable angina.
Among adults age 20 and older, the prevalence of CHD in 2004 was 15,800,000 (8,500,000 males and 7,300,000 females).
Direct medical costs of ACS are estimated at US $75 billion per year in the United States.
CHD is the single largest killer of American men and women.
CHD caused one of every five deaths in the United States in 2004.
Atherosclerosis of coronary arteries with the development of an unstable plaque and subsequent thrombosis formation.
The disease is generally thought to be an unstable clot superimposed on a fixed coronary obstruction, resulting in supply-demand mismatch.
Plaque disruption causes thrombosis in 75% of cases, while plaque erosion causes thrombosis in 25% of cases.
Macrophages are responsible for plaque disruption, neovascularization, smooth muscle apoptosis, thrombogenicity, and local inflammation.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history of premature coronary artery disease (CAD)

list.listitem: Screen adults over 18 years of age for hypertension and screen for hypercholesterolemia in men over 35 years and women over 45 years of age. A

The U.S. Protective Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends against routinely screening for coronary artery stenosis with a resting ECG, exercise treadmill test, or electron-beam CT in low-risk adults; there is insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routinely screening for coronary artery stenosis in higher risk adults. B
The USPSTF recommends against routine screening for CHD events in adults at low risk for CHD events.
The USPSTF found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine screening for CHD events in adults at increased risk for CHD events.
The USPSTF recommends screening for hypertension in adults over age 18 years and screening for lipid disorders in men older than 35 years and women older than 45 years.
The USPSTF strongly recommends that clinicians screen all adults for tobacco use and provide tobacco cessation interventions for those who use tobacco products.
The USPSTF strongly recommends that clinicians discuss aspirin chemoprevention with adults who are at increased risk for CHD.
Control blood pressure as specified by national treatment guidelines.
Treat hyperlipidemia as specified by national treatment guidelines.
Provide smoking cessation aid for all patients.
Aspirin is recommended for patients with preexisting CHD.
Blood pressure goal for patients with preexisting CHD should be less than 130/80.

Prior AHA/ACC guidelines recommended that the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) goal for patients with preexisting CHD or diabetes should be less than 70 mg/dL. Starting statin therapy within 14 days of an episode of ACS is associated with a reduction in recurrent unstable angina at four months (but has not been shown to reduce death, myocardial infarction, or stroke during this time period).
Current AHA/ACC guidelines recommend high potency statin therapy in most subjects with prior atherosclerotic vascular disease.
Provide smoking cessation aid for all patients.
Make a rapid clinical determination of the likelihood risk of obstructive CAD in all patients with chest discomfort or other symptoms suggestive of ACS. C
In patients presenting with chest discomfort or other ischemic symptoms, provide early risk stratification for the risk of cardiovascular events. C
Perform a 12-lead ECG and obtain cardiac biomarkers promptly. B
Have patients with symptoms of possible ACS transported via EMS to a hospital for evaluation. B

Differential.Differential_Features: Markedly elevated troponin, ST segment elevation
Positional change in chest pain, pericardial rub, diffuse ST elevation
Muffled heart sounds, pulsus paradoxica, low-voltage QRS
Pleuritic chest pain, unilateral absence of breath sounds, mediastinal shift
Hypoxia, pleuritic chest pain, right heart strain on ECG
Chest wall tenderness, reproduced by costochondral palpation

list.listitem: Perform a diagnostic work-up for unstable angina in patients with pressure-like substernal chest pain, radiation to jaw, neck or left upper extremity, or diaphoresis.
Male patients, especially those older than 65, patients with diaphoresis, or any patient with prior history of known CHD are at higher risk of unstable angina.

Patients whose chest pain is reproducible, pleuritic, or positional are at somewhat lower risk of unstable angina. In patients whose risk of myocardial infarction or ACS is low, the presence of chest wall pain rules out these diagnoses.

The presence or absence of cardiac risk factors such as diabetes, smoking, hypertension, or hyperlipidemia is somewhat useful in younger patients but is of little value in patients 40 to 64 years (LR+ 2.1) and of no value in patients older than age 65 years (LR+ 1.1).
ECG findings in unstable angina may include ST depression in two or more leads or may be normal.
Increasing levels of troponin I is suggestive of acute myocardial infarction. Troponin I is the preferred cardiac enzyme and should be used if available.
Combining the history and physical with high sensitivity troponin T is associated with effective triage of patients with chest pain into low, moderate, and high risk groups.

Abnormal cardiac troponin testing often does not signify an acute coronary syndrome; 1 in 8 adults presenting to emergency departments for any reason who undergo troponin testing will have elevation, but only 1.6% will have the ultimate diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction.

In patients with possible ACS who do not require cardiac catheterization, noninvasive stress testing should be performed once the patient is stable and pain free for 12 to 24 hours. There are several types of stress testing, and the choice of which to use depends on local availability and patient characteristics. Exercise stress testing is appropriate for patients who are able to walk briskly and have no baseline ECG abnormalities. Pharmacologic stress testing (eg, adenosine, dobutamine) is appropriate for patients with physical limitations. Stress echocardiography is appropriate for patients in whom there is a suspicion of structural heart disease or ventricular dysfunction.

In an observational cohort study, 64-slice coronary CT angiography was performed before admission to detect coronary plaque and stenosis (>50% luminal narrowing). Of 368 patients evaluated, 31 had ACS (8%). Investigators found that both extent of coronary plaque and presence of stenosis predicted ACS independently; only one patient with ACS had no identified calcified plaque. Half of the patients with acute chest pain and low to intermediate likelihood of ACS were free of CAD by CT and none were diagnosed with ACS (100% sensitivity).

The HEART score and the more simplified HET score can risk stratify patients with suspected unstable angina.Several clinical rules have been developed and validated to predict the risk of complications following angioplasty (CADILLAC score, Mayo score, Resnic score, Bates score, and Kimmel score).

Prognosis in unstable angina can be estimated using the TIMI risk score or modified TIMI score (adding diabetes and ejection fraction). The 6-month ACS mortality can be estimated with the Grace score.

The decision regarding invasive versus conservative management of unstable angina can be guided by a validated clinical decision rule showing which patients are most likely to benefit. A second rule predicts benefit from tirofiban.
If unstable angina is suspected, stabilize the patient, establish IV access, give oxygen and aspirin, and transport via EMS to the hospital.
Urgently obtain an ECG and troponin I, assess patient's risk status ( and/or ) and see algorithm in .
See algorithm in for treatment recommendations.
Give 325 mg of non-enteric-coated aspirin to all patients with possible unstable angina. B
Give oxygen and sublingual nitroglycerin for early treatment of suspected unstable angina; morphine may be a useful adjunct. B

For high-risk patients and selected intermediate-risk patients, give heparin (low-molecular-weight heparin [LMWH] preferred); give glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor only if percutaneous coronary intervention [PCI] is planned.
The appropriateness of an early conservative strategy or an early invasive strategy may be best determined by the severity of a patient's presentation; the TIMI risk calculator may be helpful. C

An early invasive strategy is indicated in UA/NSTEMI patients who have refractory angina or hemodynamic or electrical instability. A meta-analysis found an invasive approach best for men and high-risk women (elevated biomarkers); no benefit was found for invasive versus conservative approach for low-risk women. B
A recent meta-analysis found no evidence to support routine invasive testing versus conservative management in affecting all cause mortality measured at 10 years.

See algorithm in for an overview of treatment. The AHA/ACC guidelines recommend either a conservative or early invasive strategy for those at high risk for ACS. A validated clinical rule uses risk stratification to assist in this decision.
Anti-thrombotic agents

Aspirin 165 mg to 325 mg (non-enteric-coated) reduces mortality in ACS over the first 35 days after presentation (absolute risk reduction [ARR] 2.6%, NNT = 40) and is recommended for all patients as a loading dose followed by daily low dose aspirin. Clopidogrel also reduces death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, or stroke when used in definite UA/NSTEMI (ARR = 2.1%). Ongoing studies are evaluating the best duration of dual antiplatelet therapy in subjects who have received bare-metal or drug-eluting stents, with some studies suggesting that prolonged clopidogrel therapy may be of no added therapy to a shorter duration.

ACC guidelines (2025) make the following recommendations for initial selection of an oral P2Y12 inhibitor based on treatment selected:
Percutaneous coronary intervention (NSTEMI and STEMI): aspirin + (ticagrelor or prasugrel) Coronary artery bypass graft (CABG): aspirin + (ticagrelor or clopidogrel started post-op) No planned invasive intervention: aspirin + ticagrelor Fibrinolytic (STEMI): aspirin + clopidogrel

However, a subsequent study randomized 2201 patients who underwent CABG for treatment of acute coronary syndrome to aspirin + ticagrelor or aspirin alone post-operatively. There was no reduction in the composite of death, MI, stroke or repeat revascularization with combination therapy, and an increased risk of major bleeding (4.9% vs 2.0%, HR 2.5, 95% CI 1.5 to 4.1).

ACC guidelines (2025) recommend parenteral anticoagulation for all patients with acute coronary syndrome. Unfractionated heparin (UFH) is recommended for most patients. If early invasive strategy (PCI or CABG) is not anticipated, then enoxaparin or fondaprinux are alternatives to UFH. Continue parenteral anticoagaulation until the time of PCI or CABG. For patients undergoing PCI for STEMI, bivalirudin is an alternative to UFH. It may be reasonable in patients with NSTEMI as well.

Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors have the greatest effect in conjunction with angioplasty; ACC guidelines (2025) recommend against their routine use in patients with ACS outside of selected patients with PCI. A clinical decision rule can predict the likelihood of benefit. When administered during PCI, glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors reduce death and recurrent MI and death at 30 days and 6 months at the expense of increased major bleeding. When started as initial medical therapy in ACS (i.e., without PCI), however, there is no mortality benefit with glycoprotein IIb/IIIa use.
ACC guidelines (2025) recommend IV or intracoronary glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor in patients undergoing PCI with a large thrombus burden, no-reflow, or slow flow to reduce infarct size.

The ACC/AHA Joint Task Force recommends that statins be prescribed for patients before hospital discharge after an episode of ACS based on the results of two RCTs showing a reduced composite endpoint (death, myocardial infarction, rehospitalization) or event rate (2.6% and 3.9% absolute RRs). This recommendation is still the subject of debate.

Intensive stain therapy (simvastatin 80 mg/day) decreased overall mortality rates compared with lower doses in patients with a recent history of ACS (3.5% vs 4.6%, respectively; NNT = 20 to prevent 1 additional death over 2 years). Analysis of 18 studies, however, do not demonstrate reduction in death, myocardial infarction, or stroke for the first four months after an acute coronary syndrome. Occurrences of unstable angina may be reduced after four months follow up. (Current guidelines do not recommend routine use of high dose simvastatin [80 mg/day] because of concerns for toxicity.)
Nitrates do not decrease mortality when used in suspected acute myocardial infarction.
Beta-blockers reduce overall vascular mortality (ARR 1.3%) when used in suspected acute myocardial infarction.
Nondihydropyridine calcium channel blockers decrease recurrent nonfatal myocardial infarction but not mortality when used in acute myocardial infarction.

According to the AHA/ACC guidelines, diagnostic cardiac catheterization with percutaneous intervention (if indicated) is appropriate as part of an early invasive treatment strategy or if a patient develops high-risk criteria. An early invasive strategy is associated with reduced refractory angina, rehospitalization, and late myocardial infarction even though procedure-related complications (bleeding, infarction) are higher.
The decision to perform bypass surgery is based on the catheterization findings.

In a RCT of immediate versus next day (21 hour deferral) intervention for 352 patients with ACS without ST-segment elevation and a TIMI score of 3 or more, there was no difference in MI between groups peak troponin or a composite of death, myocardial infarction, or urgent revascularization at 1-month follow-up (13.7% vs 10.2%, respectively).

A similar study of 251 patients (interim analysis) with non-ST-segment elevation ACS however found an increased rate of MI in comparison with a 24-48 h deferred strategy, despite aggressive antithrombotic treatment; the rates of MI however were very high in this study (60% vs 38%).

In a larger RCT of immediate versus delayed intervention (≥36 hours) in over 3,000 high-risk patients, there was no difference in the primary composite endpoint (death, myocardial infarction, or stroke at 6 months) but results favored early intervention for the secondary composite endpoint (death, myocardial infarction, or refractory ischemia) (9.5% vs 12.9%).

A meta-analysis identified 4 RCTs with 1126 patients over the age of 70 years with NSTEMI. Invasive strategies resulted in fewer cardiovascular events (OR 0.60, 95% CI 0.40 - 0.91) and fewer unplanned revascularizations (OR 0.31, 95% CI 0.15-0.64) but no change in all cause mortality or bleeding complications.
Complete revascularization after STEMI is associated with fewer recurrent MI.
If unstable angina is suspected, evaluation and treatment should always take place in an emergency department or hospital setting.
If a patient presents with chest pain or other symptoms that could be ACS, they should be transported via EMS.
The major complication of unstable angina is acute myocardial infarction; see that topic for management.
Chest pain units improve outcomes in unstable angina.
Patients who are admitted should have continuous ECG monitoring/telemetry, oxygen, IV access, bed rest, and serial cardiac enzymes testing.
A study using a large inpatient database found no association between having an EGD or colonoscopy during an admission for ACS and mortality.
The Grace score and TIMI risk score (see ) can be used to estimate the prognosis of individuals with a recent episode of unstable angina. C
With proper treatment, the risk of myocardial infarction or death after unstable angina can be reduced significantly. A
In a 1973 observational study, patients with (untreated) unstable angina had a 1-year mortality of 43% and a 10-year mortality of 81%.
Prognosis varies since the diagnosis of unstable angina covers a wide spectrum of presentations.
The AHA/ACC risk stratification guidelines or the TIMI Risk Score for UA/NSTEMI provide an estimation of the risk of recurrent MI or death (low, intermediate, high).
The Grace score is another validated tool for predicting 6-month prognosis.
A meta-analysis of systemic anticoagulation therapy in UA/NSTEMI showed the risk for mortality was decreased with LMWH compared with UFH (ARR 1.5%).
Among patients with ACS who undergo PCI, the development of an MI unrelated to PCI is a predictor of subsequent mortality; in contrast, periprocedural MI was not associated with mortality.
According to the INTERHEART study, modifiable risk factors account for over 90% of the risk for myocardial infarction.
Advise patients to stop smoking; exercise; achieve ideal body weight; and eat a plant-based, whole foods diet.

Monitoring only; individualized treatment unless patient develops intermediate- or high-risk criteria.
NTG- Beta blockers. Consider: Clopidogrel, Heparin (UFH or LMWH), Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor.
NTG- Beta blockers, Heparin (UFH or LMWH), Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa if PCI planned or if abnormal ECG or elevated troponin Consider: Clopidogrel if no CABG; PCI if early invasive strategy.

Early conservative strategy for high risk: Use clopidogrel, Consider glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor. Cardiac catheterization indicated if: Refractory ischemic chest pain, Recurrent/persistent ST deviation, Ventricular tachycardia, Hemodynamic instability, Signs of pump failure.

Early invasive strategy for high risk: To catheterization lab to define anatomy and perform PCI if indicated, Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitor should be used, Clopidogrel can be safely used if PCI but not CABG.
